params.question: Based on the NFHS-5 findings discussed in the narration, why is merely making health information available insufficient to change behaviour in rural India?

answers.text: Rural populations lack interest in health-related matters

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration does not attribute the gap to lack of interest. NFHS-5 identifies low health literacy — the capacity to understand, process, and act on health information — as the barrier, not motivation.

answers.text: The method of communication determines whether information translates into behaviour change

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration explicitly states that 'how information is communicated determines whether behaviour changes.' The ORS vignette illustrates this — the same message succeeded via demonstration but failed via pamphlet.

answers.text: Health workers at sub-centres are not trained to deliver health education

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration does not cite health-worker training as the issue. The ANM did visit the mother three times — the problem was the choice of method (a text-heavy pamphlet), not a lack of training.

answers.text: Printed materials are always ineffective in community settings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is an overgeneralisation. The narration critiques one specific pamphlet ('too many words') but does not claim all print materials are ineffective — rather, that the method must match the audience.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the narration: the health literacy gap identified by NFHS-5 means that simply making information available does not guarantee behaviour change. The choice of communication method is what determines whether the audience actually changes knowledge, attitudes, and practices.

Well done. Park defines health education as a process affecting changes in knowledge, attitudes, and practices. The NFHS-5 data and the ORS vignette together demonstrate that the communication method — not just the content — is the decisive factor.

params.question: According to the narration on organising health promotion activities (CM4.2), which of the following correctly describes the primary activity at the individual and family level?

answers.text: Group counselling sessions conducted at the Primary Health Centre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Group counselling at the PHC falls under the clinical setting, not the individual/family setting. The family-level activity is delivered in the home, not at a health facility.

answers.text: Health exhibition organised by the district health office

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Health exhibitions are a community-level mass method aimed at reaching large audiences. They do not provide the one-to-one engagement characteristic of the individual/family setting.

answers.text: Structured home visit by ANMs and ASHAs under Medical Officer supervision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration identifies the home visit — with advance preparation, rapport establishment, and follow-up — as the primary activity at the individual and family level, conducted by ANMs and ASHAs under the MO's supervision.

answers.text: Street play performed by trained folk media artists

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Street plays (folk media) are a community-level mass method used for awareness generation. They reach large audiences but lack the personalised depth of the home visit.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration describes three settings mandated by CM4.2. At the individual/family level, the primary activity is the structured home visit by ANMs and ASHAs, involving advance preparation, rapport building, and follow-up — not a facility-based or mass-reach method.

Exactly. The structured home visit is the cornerstone of individual and family-level health promotion — it allows personalised assessment, rapport, and follow-up tailored to the household's specific needs.

params.question: You are a medical student about to conduct your first health education session at a FAP centre for a group of mothers. Which action best demonstrates correct introductory facilitation as described in the narration?

answers.text: Begin presenting key health messages immediately to maximise teaching time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Skipping the introductory phase undermines rapport and participation. The narration allocates a dedicated five minutes for introductions precisely because rushing into content leads to passive, unengaged audiences.

answers.text: Distribute a written pre-test questionnaire as the very first activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While pre-testing is part of session design (CM4.3), the narration places introduction and rapport before any assessment. Starting with a written test can intimidate low-literacy participants and impair trust.

answers.text: Introduce yourself by role, establish ground rules that all questions are welcome, and use an icebreaker

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration specifies Step 1: welcome participants, introduce yourself by role ('I am your medical student… here to learn with you'), establish ground rules (discussion format, no wrong answers), and use an icebreaker for new groups.

answers.text: Ask participants to read the educational pamphlet silently before beginning discussion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This mirrors the failed approach from the opening vignette — a text-heavy, passive method. The narration emphasises active facilitation with verbal introduction, ground-rule setting, and participatory icebreakers.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the facilitation steps from the narration: Step 1 is Introduction and Rapport (5 minutes) — introduce yourself by role (not just name), establish ground rules (discussion, all questions welcome, no wrong answers), and use an icebreaker. This sets the tone for the entire session.

Well done. CM4.4 emphasises that conducting a session is a distinct competency from designing one. The introductory phase — role clarity, ground rules, icebreaker — sets the participatory tone that determines whether the session achieves genuine engagement.

interactions.label: A district immunisation awareness campaign raised mothers' knowledge of vaccine

params.question: A district immunisation awareness campaign raised mothers' knowledge of vaccine schedules from 40% to 85%, yet immunisation coverage remained at 62%. Using the KAP framework from the narration, which analysis best explains this discrepancy?

answers.text: The knowledge assessment tool was poorly designed and overestimated actual learning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While measurement validity is a general concern, the narration's KAP framework explains this pattern as a normal phenomenon — knowledge is the easiest to change, and a measured gain can be genuine yet still not translate into practice change.

answers.text: Knowledge change was achieved, but attitudinal and structural barriers prevented practice change

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration states that in the KAP sequence, each level is harder to change than the previous one. Knowledge gain (easiest) does not automatically overcome attitudinal barriers or structural obstacles like distance, vaccine availability, or family opposition.

answers.text: The campaign used mass methods when it should have used individual counselling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While method choice matters, the KAP framework addresses a deeper issue: even a well-chosen method may change knowledge without changing practice if attitudinal and structural barriers remain. Method selection alone does not explain the K-P gap.

answers.text: The target population was too large for any single campaign to influence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Population size affects reach, not the K-to-P conversion. The KAP framework explains that knowledge, attitudes, and practices form a sequential hierarchy — success at one level does not guarantee success at the next, regardless of population size.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration explains the KAP evaluation framework: Knowledge is easiest to change, Attitude harder, and Practice hardest. An immunisation campaign can successfully improve knowledge while leaving vaccination rates unchanged because structural and attitudinal barriers — not information deficits — are blocking the behaviour change.

Exactly. The KAP framework reveals that Knowledge → Attitude → Practice is a sequential hierarchy, with each step harder to achieve. Evaluation must measure all three levels, not assume that a knowledge gain will automatically produce behaviour change.
